entry: Tenth month of the year in the Julian and [[Gregorian calendar|Gregorian]] calendars, with 31 days. Its name comes from [[Latin]] *octō*, "eight," because it was the eighth month of the early calendar of ancient Rome, before January and February were added. Among the Anglo-Saxons it was called Winterfylleth, because winter was supposed to begin at its full moon. The month falls in autumn in parts of the Northern Hemisphere and in spring in the Southern Hemisphere. Its birthstones are tourmaline and opal. [[Halloween]] is observed on October 31.

Soft-bodied, eight-limbed mollusc of the order Octopoda. Its some 300 species are grouped within the class [[Cephalopod|Cephalopoda]], with squids, cuttlefish and nautiloids. The giant Pacific octopus (*Enteroctopus dofleini*) is often cited as the largest species, with adults usually weighing 10–50 kg and arm spans of up to 4.8 m. Octopuses have a complex nervous system and excellent sight, and are among the most intelligent invertebrates. They live in habitats from [[Coral reef|coral reefs]] to the seabed and abyssal depths. Most species grow quickly, mature early and are short-lived; the male dies soon after mating, and the female dies after her eggs hatch. Octopuses hunt crustaceans, bivalves, gastropods and fish. They defend themselves by expelling ink, using [[Camouflage|camouflage]], threat displays and jet propulsion. All octopuses are [[Venom|venomous]], but only the [[Blue-ringed octopus|blue-ringed octopuses]] are known to be deadly to humans.

Japanese [[Samurai|samurai]] and *daimyō* regarded as the first of the three great unifiers of Japan. He was head of the powerful Oda clan of Owari Province and, through a series of wars against other *daimyō* beginning in the 1560s, became the most powerful of them. He overthrew the nominally ruling [[Shogun|shogun]] Ashikaga Yoshiaki in 1573, dissolving the Ashikaga shogunate, and conquered most of [[Honshu]] by 1580. His rule was noted for innovative military tactics, fostering of free trade and reforms of civil government, but also for the brutal suppression of those who refused to cooperate. He was a leading figure of the [[Sengoku period]] and of the Azuchi–Momoyama period, named for his castle at Azuchi and for Momoyama, where Hideyoshi retired. In the Honnō-ji Incident, his retainer Akechi Mitsuhide ambushed him in a temple in [[Kyoto]], and Nobunaga committed seppuku. [[Toyotomi Hideyoshi]] defeated Mitsuhide and, with [[Tokugawa Ieyasu]], completed the unification of Japan.

Type of lyric poem that praises or glorifies an event or individual, or describes nature intellectually and emotionally. Odes originated in [[Ancient Greece]], where they were performed to musical accompaniment, usually on the aulos or the [[Lyre|lyre]]. Three typical forms are recognized. Pindaric odes follow the style of the poet Pindar and have a three-part structure of strophe, antistrophe and epode. Horatian odes follow the conventions of the Roman poet [[Horace]], with stanzas that share one rhyme scheme and meter, and often treat intimate subjects such as love and friendship. Irregular odes use rhyme but neither the three-part form nor fixed stanzas. [[William Wordsworth|Wordsworth]]'s "Ode on Intimations of Immortality" (1807) is written in the Pindaric style, and [[John Keats|Keats]] wrote "Ode to a Nightingale" (1819) in the Horatian form.

City (pop., 2021: about 1,010,537) and major seaport in southwestern [[Ukraine]], on the northwestern shore of the [[Black Sea]]. Also spelled Odessa, it is the administrative center of Odesa Oblast and the third-most populous city in Ukraine. A Greek settlement existed there by the middle of the 6th century BC. The site was part of the [[Ottoman Empire]] from 1529 until 1792. In 1794 a decree of Catherine II established a naval harbor and trading place at Khadjibey, soon renamed Odessa. From 1819 to 1858 it was a free port, and in the 19th century it was the fourth-largest city of the [[Russian Empire]]. Its architecture, heavily influenced by French and Italian styles, is more Mediterranean than Russian. The city hosts Ukraine's largest seaport, which handles around 60 percent of the nation's exports, and an oil terminal at Port Pivdennyi. On January 25, 2023, its historic center was declared a [[World Heritage Site]] and added to the List of World Heritage in Danger by [[UNESCO]], in response to bombing during the Russian invasion of Ukraine.

[[Indo-Aryan languages|Indo-Aryan]] language spoken mainly in the Indian state of [[Odisha]]. Native speakers make up 82% of Odisha's population, and the language is also spoken in parts of [[West Bengal]], Jharkhand, [[Andhra Pradesh]] and [[Chhattisgarh]]. It is one of India's official languages and the sixth Indian language to be designated a classical language, in 2014. Odia descends from Odra Prakrit, which evolved from Magadhi Prakrit, and has passed through the stages Proto-Odia (7th–9th century CE), Old Odia (10th–13th century CE), Middle Odia (14th–17th century CE) and Modern Odia (from the 18th century). The earliest known Old Odia inscription, the Urajam inscription of the Eastern Gangas, dates to 1051 CE. In the 15th century Sarala Das translated the Mahabharata into Odia. The language shows influence from tribal and Dravidian tongues and has an unbroken literary tradition, with inscriptions more than a thousand years old.

Widely revered god of the dead and of warfare in [[Norse mythology]] and [[Germanic paganism]]. He is head of the pantheon of the Æsir, bearing a spear and a ring, and is husband of Frigg and father of [[Thor]]. He is often depicted as long-bearded and one-eyed, having sacrificed an eye for wisdom, and is accompanied by the ravens Huginn and Muninn and the wolves Geri and Freki. In myth he receives slain warriors, the einherjar, in Valhöll, and the [[Poetic Edda]] associates him with the [[Valkyrie|Valkyries]]. At Ragnarök he leads the einherjar and is killed by the wolf Fenrir. Early travelers described [[Human sacrifice|human sacrifices]] made to him, and in later folklore he leads the Wild Hunt. Most forms of [[Heathenry (new religious movement)|Heathenry]] venerate him, and his name is given to Wednesday in many languages.

State in eastern [[India]], spelled Orissa until 2011. It is the eighth-largest state by area, with over 41 million inhabitants. Its 485 km of coastline lie on the [[Bay of Bengal]]. The ancient kingdom of Kalinga, invaded by the Mauryan emperor [[Ashoka]] in 261 BCE, coincides with the modern borders. The Orissa Province was established on April 1, 1936. Cuttack served as the capital until 1948, when [[Bhubaneswar]] replaced it. The state's language is [[Odia language|Odia]].

Order of predatory flying insects that includes [[Dragonfly|dragonflies]] and [[Damselfly|damselflies]]. Odonates have large compound eyes, two pairs of long, transparent wings that move independently, and elongated abdomens. Adults catch prey in flight with specialized legs, and they can land and perch. Almost all have aquatic [[Nymph (biology)|nymphs]] called naiads, which are carnivorous and eat anything they can overpower, including small [[Fish|fish]]. Dragonflies (Anisoptera) have bulkier bodies and hold their wings horizontal at rest, while damselflies (Zygoptera) have slender bodies and close their wings. The order also includes three relict damsel-dragonflies (Anisozygoptera). Johan Christian Fabricius coined the name Odonata in 1793, from the Greek word for tooth. Its lineage traces to the Paleozoic era, and the scientific study of these insects is called odonatology.

Smell caused by volatilized chemical compounds, usually present in low concentrations, that humans and many animals perceive through the [[Olfactory system|olfactory system]]. Commonwealth English spells it odour. The terms scent, aroma and fragrance usually denote pleasant odors. Odorant molecules bind to receptor proteins on the cilia of olfactory receptor neurons in the olfactory epithelium, a small patch of tissue at the back of the nasal cavity. The resulting signals travel along the olfactory nerve to the olfactory bulb, where the smell is interpreted in relation to past experience. The brain identifies a smell from patterns of signals across many receptor types, not from any single compound. Most odors are [[Organic compound|organic compounds]], though [[Hydrogen sulfide]] and [[Ammonia]] are also odorants. Women usually outperform men in odor discrimination, although a 2019 meta-analysis found the difference to be small. Pregnant women have heightened sensitivity to smell.

Ancient Thracian state of the eastern [[Balkans]], flourishing from the early 5th century BC. It was the first large political entity to develop in the region. Teres I founded the kingdom by exploiting the collapse of the Persian presence in Europe after Persia's failed invasion of Greece in 480–479 BC. Teres and his son Sitalces expanded it into one of the most powerful states of its time. It was an ally of [[Athens]] and joined the [[Peloponnesian War]] on Athens's side. A brief revival under Cotys I ended with his murder. The kingdom then divided among three Odrysian kings and was conquered by [[Macedonia (ancient kingdom)|Macedon]] under Philip II in 340 BC. A smaller state centered on Seuthopolis, founded around 330 BC, lasted until the second quarter of the 3rd century BC. Its heartland later became the Sapaean kingdom, a client of the [[Roman Republic]] that was converted into the Roman province of Thracia in 45–46 AD.

Legendary Greek king of Ithaca and hero of [[Homer]]'s *Odyssey*, known in [[Latin]] as Ulysses. He is the son of Laërtes and Anticlea, husband of Penelope and father of Telemachus, and is renowned for his cunning and resourcefulness, described in Greek as *polytropos*, meaning of many turns. He is most famous for his *nostos*, or homecoming, which took ten years after the decade-long [[Trojan War]]. On the journey he outwits the Cyclops Polyphemus and resists the [[Siren (mythology)|Sirens]]. Back on Ithaca he returns disguised as a beggar to take revenge on suitors who have overrun his palace. Later accounts credit him with devising the [[Trojan Horse]] that led to the fall of [[Troy]].

Ancient Greek epic poem attributed to [[Homer]], one of two great epics with the *Iliad*. It is among the oldest surviving works of literature and is divided into 24 books. It follows [[Odysseus]], king of Ithaca, on his homecoming after the [[Trojan War]]. The journey takes ten years, during which he encounters many perils and all of his crewmates are killed. In his absence his wife Penelope and son Telemachus contend with suitors competing for Penelope's hand. The poem was first composed in Homeric Greek around the 8th or 7th century BC and was part of the Greek literary canon by the mid-6th century BC. Scholars predominantly assume it was composed within long oral traditions. Its themes include *nostos* (homecoming), *xenia* (guest-friendship) and testing. The first complete English translation appeared in 1616. In 2018, a poll of experts by [[BBC]] Culture found it to be literature's most enduring narrative.

Mythical Greek king of Thebes and tragic hero. Oedipus unwittingly fulfilled a prophecy that he would kill his father and marry his mother. Without knowing their identities, he killed Laius at a crossroads, then solved the riddle of the [[Sphinx]], winning the throne and the hand of Jocasta. Years later, when a plague struck Thebes, he discovered that he himself was responsible. Jocasta hanged herself, and Oedipus blinded himself. The legend is best known from the plays of [[Sophocles]], and [[Sigmund Freud|Freud]] used it to name the [[Oedipus complex]].

Athenian [[Tragedy|tragedy]] by [[Sophocles]], also called *Oedipus Tyrannus* or *Oedipus the King*. It is thought to have been first performed c. 429 BC, though this is uncertain. It won only second place at its premiere, but [[Aristotle]] later considered it one of the greatest Greek tragedies, and it is now regarded as one of the greatest plays of Western literature. The play concerns Oedipus's search for the murderer of King Laius to end a [[Plague (disease)|plague]] on Thebes, unaware that he himself is the killer. As the truth emerges, Jocasta hangs herself, and Oedipus, horrified at his patricide and incest, gouges out his own eyes. In the order of events it comes before *Oedipus at Colonus* and *Antigone*, although it was written about a dozen years after *Antigone*. Aristotle discusses it several times in his *Poetics*.

Concept in [[Sigmund Freud|Freud]]'s psychoanalytic theory of a son's sexual desire for his mother and hostility toward his father. Freud introduced the term in a 1910 paper. He considered identification with the same-sex parent the socially acceptable outcome, and failure to move on from the complex a cause of neurosis. The name derives from the myth of [[Oedipus]]. Freud rejected the Electra complex, introduced by [[Carl Jung]] in 1913. Some critics argue that, by replacing his seduction theory with this one, Freud helped cover up child sexual abuse.

1937 novella by American author [[John Steinbeck]]. It follows George Milton and Lennie Small, migrant ranch workers who move from job to job in [[California]] during the [[Great Depression]]. They dream of owning a farm, but Lennie, who is intellectually disabled, depends on George. Steinbeck drew on his own experiences as a teenager working alongside migrant farm workers. The title comes from a line of [[Robert Burns]]'s poem "To a Mouse." The novella is frequently challenged or banned for what some consider offensive and racist language, and it appears on the American Library Association's list of the most challenged books of the 21st century.

Fifth studio album by [[Michael Jackson]], released by Epic Records in 1979. It was the first album Jackson made for Epic and the first produced by [[Quincy Jones]]. Drawing on disco, pop, funk, R&B and soft rock, it features songs by [[Stevie Wonder]], [[Paul McCartney]] and [[David Foster]]. Two of its five singles, "Don't Stop 'Til You Get Enough" and "Rock with You," reached number one on the Billboard Hot 100. The album has sold over 20 million copies worldwide. It received two [[Grammy Awards]] nominations, and Jackson won Best R&B Vocal Performance, Male, for "Don't Stop 'Til You Get Enough."

Space in which the members of an organization perform administrative work. The word derives from Latin *officium*, which originally referred to a staff member or formal position as much as to a place. In [[Classical antiquity|classical antiquity]], offices were often part of a palace complex or temple, with rooms where scribes kept scrolls. In the High Middle Ages the chancery of a kingdom wrote and stored government letters and laws, in walls of pigeonholes. The first purpose-built offices appeared in the 18th century. With the [[Industrial Revolution]], banking, rail, insurance, retail, petroleum and [[Telegraphy|telegraphy]] required many clerks. The "Modern Efficiency Desk" of 1915 had a flat top and drawers below, so that managers could easily watch their workers. By the mid-20th century, cubicles evolved to provide privacy. Later designs include open plans, hot-desking and hybrid models, and remote work accelerated during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Member of an armed force who holds a position of authority, usually a commissioned officer. The term broadly covers commissioned, non-commissioned and warrant officers, but without qualification it usually refers only to commissioned officers, who derive their authority from a commission from the [[Head of state|head of state]]. Commissioned officers typically make up between an eighth and a fifth of modern armed forces personnel. In the First World War fewer than 5% of British soldiers were officers. Many militaries require a university degree for commissioning, but the [[Israel Defense Forces]] and the British Armed Forces do not, although many of their officers are graduates. In the United Kingdom, officers enter directly from military academy, through service entry from the senior non-commissioned ranks, or through late entry at age 30 or older. Commissioned officers typically receive training in leadership and management in addition to their military specialty.

Synthetic chemical element (symbol Og) with atomic number 118, the heaviest known element. It was first synthesized at the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research in Dubna, near [[Moscow]], by a team of Russian and American scientists. It was formally named in 2016 after the nuclear physicist Yuri Oganessian, who led the discovery of the heaviest elements. It belongs to group 18, the [[Noble gas|noble gases]], but its only known isotope has a half-life of 0.7 ms, too short for chemical studies. Theoretical studies predict that relativistic effects would make it a solid at room temperature.

U.S. state in the Midwest, bordering [[Lake Erie]]. Admitted in 1803, it was the first state admitted under the Northwest Ordinance and the first post-colonial free state admitted to the Union. Its capital and most populous city is Columbus. The name comes from the [[Ohio River]], from a Seneca word meaning "good river." Ohio has the third-largest manufacturing sector in the U.S. It is nicknamed the Buckeye State and was the birthplace of seven U.S. presidents. The [[Wright brothers]] designed and built the world's first successful airplane in Ohio, though its first flight took place in North Carolina.

River of the eastern United States, 1,579 km long and the largest tributary of the [[Mississippi River]] by volume. It flows southwest from [[Pittsburgh]], Pennsylvania, to the Mississippi at Cairo, Illinois, forming the boundary between the Midwestern and Southern United States. Its basin includes parts of 14 states and supplies drinking water to five million people. Rapids at the Falls of the Ohio near Louisville restricted large commercial navigation until the Louisville and Portland Canal bypassed them in 1830. Since the canalization of the river in 1929 it has been divided into 21 pools by 20 [[Lock (water navigation)|locks]] and dams. The name comes from a Seneca word meaning "good river," and [[Thomas Jefferson]] called the river "the most beautiful river on earth." It is also one of the most polluted rivers in the United States.

Class of U.S. Navy nuclear-powered submarines, the largest ever built for the U.S. Navy. The class comprises 14 ballistic missile submarines (SSBNs) and four [[Cruise missile|cruise missile]] submarines (SSGNs). Each displaces 18,750 tons submerged and can carry 24 Trident II ballistic missiles. The SSBNs form part of the nuclear-deterrent triad alongside strategic bombers and [[Intercontinental ballistic missile|intercontinental ballistic missiles]], and together carry about half of U.S. active strategic thermonuclear warheads. All but one, USS Henry M. Jackson, are named for [[U.S. state|U.S. states]], a tradition the Navy previously reserved for battleships and cruisers.

Unit of electrical resistance in the [[International System of Units|SI]], symbol Ω, named for German physicist [[Georg Ohm]]. One ohm is the resistance between two points of a conductor when a constant potential difference of one [[Volt|volt]] produces a current of one [[Ampere|ampere]] in it. Since the 2019 revision of the SI, the ohm has been defined exactly in terms of fundamental constants. Its reciprocal, the [[Siemens (unit)|siemens]], is the unit of conductance. Telegraphers in the 19th century needed a practical standard for resistance, and the British Association for the Advancement of Science proposed a unit as early as 1861. The power dissipated by a resistor is P = VI = V²/R = I²R.
